sentences.text: Baru is an extinct genus of mekosuchine crocodile from Australia.
This animal possessed an incredibly deep and robust skull with long teeth featuring compressed crowns and minute serrations in the case of B. darrowi.

Some researchers describe the Baru skull as altirostral, a term meaning high-snouted, distinguishing it from the low-snouted shape of generalist crocodilians like Paludirex, Kambara, and Australosuchus.
The sides of the mandibular ramus of Baru are heavily sculpted.
Baru possessed slightly recurved teeth that varied greatly in size.
Baru was among the larger mekosuchines, with adult skulls reaching 50 cm in length.
A 1997 review estimated Baru adults reached a length of around 4 meters.
The largest known skull of Baru iylwenpeny measured 58.8 cm.
Based on its size and build, researchers speculate that Baru darrowi could hunt prey weighing up to 300 kg, including similarly sized crocodiles.
The genus Baru was described by Willis et al. in 1990.
Baru was among the first mekosuchines described, with B. darrowi named in 1990 based on fossils from the Northern Territory and Queensland.
B. darrowi was named after English actor Paul Darrow in tribute to his contributions to Riversleigh research.
The Alcoota material was recognized as a distinct species named B. iylwenpeny and unveiled in 2023.
Fossils of Baru have been found in Riversleigh in northwestern Queensland and at Alcoota Station in the Northern Territory, Australia.
Baru's skull functioned like a cleaver, using large, backward-facing teeth and jaw festooning to deliver incapacitating blows to prey.
The interlocking festooning of Baru's jaws drove an enlarged fourth lower tooth into prey, generating shearing and breaking forces capable of piercing armor.
Minute serrations on the teeth of Baru darrowi likely helped cut through flesh and tissue as struggling prey resisted the bite.
Due to its shallow-water habitat, Baru likely evolved a powerful bite to quickly immobilize prey and prevent escape.
Willis suggests Baru hunted in shallower waters than modern saltwater crocodiles, making the drowning method of killing less effective.
Fossils from Bullock Creek and Riversleigh show bite marks from crocodilians like Baru on flightless birds such as Dromornis and Emuarius, and large marsupials like Neohelos.
Baru lived in freshwater lagoons within humid forests and hunted prey by ambush, similar to modern crocodiles.
Willis suggested that Baru may have inhabited shallower waters like freshwater lakes and streams within its range.
The second premaxillary tooth was gradually reduced and lost as Baru aged.
Juveniles of Baru iylwenpeny had more compressed teeth than adults, with anterior teeth becoming circular in cross-section while posterior teeth remained only mildly flattened.
Three species are recognized: B. darrowi (type species), B. iylwenpeny, and B. wickeni.
Baru is typically classified as a derived mekosuchine related to the semi-aquatic Paludirex.
A phylogenetic analysis of Baru iylwenpeny placed Mekosuchus as the closest relative to the Paludirex-Baru clade, differing from other studies.
B. iylwenpeny is noted for its robustness, which exceeds that of other species in the genus.
Baru fossils date from the Late Oligocene to the Late Miocene.
B. darrowi reached 4 meters in length and dates to the Middle Miocene.
Fossils of Baru date from the Late Oligocene to the Middle Miocene.
Baru wickeni is known exclusively from the D Site and Whitehunter Site within Faunal Zone A of the Riversleigh deposits.
Baru eventually went extinct due to climate changes in Australia during the Late Miocene.
One hypothesis suggests a devastating pulse of aridification destroyed Baru's preferred habitat before conditions improved in the Pliocene.
It is debated whether Baru teeth are ziphodont, as recent studies argue their crenulation is too fine for that classification.
